The aim of the following code is to broadly describe the data before diving into a more specific analysis.

### Loading libraries and the data

```{r}
#| message: false
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))
```

#### Exploring the patients

From the data cleaning, we know that there are 1610 patients in this data set.

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(sex, status) |> 
  count() |>
  group_by(sex) |> 
  mutate(percentage = (n/sum(n))*100)
```

The patients in this study are about two thirds men to one third women, with roughly a 50% survival rate, though survival of women is slightly lower than that of men on first inspection.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
p1 <- clinical_augment |> 
        ggplot(aes(x = sex,
                   fill = status))+
        geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(x= "",
       y = "Number of patients",
       fill = "Status",
       title = "Profiles of the patients in the cancer study")+
  theme_minimal()
p2 <- ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = status,
                     y = sex,
                     colour = age_group))+
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10)+
  geom_count(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(size = "Count",
       x = "Status",
       y = "",
       colour = "Age")+
  theme_minimal()

p1+p2+ plot_layout(widths = c(1, 5))
```

Few patients are under 30 years old, with most in the 61-70 age group. **WHAT CAN BE SAID ABOUT THE POSITION OF THE DOTS ON THE GRID ?**

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(cancer_type, sex) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = cancer_type,
             fill = sex))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1))+
  labs(x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of affected patients",
       fill = "Sex",
       title = "Number of patients affected by each type of cancer")
```

Eleven types of cancer are tracked in this data set, two of which (breast cancer and skin cancer, non-melanoma) affect only women or men respectively. Only one patient is affected by skin cancer.

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  filter(status == "DECEASED") |> 
  group_by(age_group, cancer_type) |>
  summarise(average_survival_months = mean(os_months)) |> 
  arrange(average_survival_months) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group,
             y = average_survival_months,
             colour = cancer_type))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x = "Age group",
       y = "Average survival (months)",
       colour = "Cancer type",
       title = "Average survival per cancer type")
```

Across age groups, melanoma and renal cell carcinoma are associated with higher survival than other cancer types, expect for the \<30 age group, where renal cell carcinoma is associated with the shortest survival time. The majority of cancer types seem to have an average survival time between 5 and 15 months. Patients under 30 years old have the shortest average survival time, while the patients between 50 and 60 have the longest on average.

#### Exploring the types of mutations

Visualizing the number of mutations that affect each patient.

```{r}
ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = cancer_type,
                     y = total_mutations,
                     color = cancer_type)) +
  geom_jitter() +
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "Cancer type and number of mutations", 
       subtitle = "The dots indicate how many mutations the individual patient has",
       x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of mutations") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**EXPLANATION**

```{r}
clinical_mutation |> 
  filter(is_top_gene) |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hugo_symbol,
             fill = cancer_type))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(title = "Number of mutations associated to top 20 genes",
       x = "Hugo symbol of affected gene",
       y = "Number of mutations",
       fill = "Cancer type")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1))
```

There are big variations in the number of genes with mutations. The TP53 gene is the most mutated gene in this data set and appears in all the cancer types.

```{r}
mutation_augment |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  count(name = "nbr_occurences") |>
  ungroup() |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(nbr_occurences),
            max = max(nbr_occurences),
            min = min(nbr_occurences),
            median = median(nbr_occurences))
```

This table summarizes the number of mutations affecting each gene. This shows the considerable variation in how genes are affected in all types of cancer.

## Location of mutations in the genome

```{r}
clinical_mutation |>
  arrange(chromosome) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = chromosome,
             fill = age_group))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x = "Chromosome",
       y = "Number of mutations",
       fill = "Age group",
       title = "Location of mutations in chromosomes")
```

This graph shows the location of the mutations with respect to the chromosomes. The most affected chromosome is number 17, while the least affected is number 21. There are no mutations associated to the Y chromosome in this data set. Age does not seem to have much impact on the location of the mutation.
